summary: Defines a set of metrics, called Precision Availability Metrics (PAMs), for network services that have performance targets written as Service Level Objectives (SLOs). They help providers and customers check whether a service, such as a network slice service from RFC 9543, is meeting its promised performance.

plainLanguage.summary: If a pizza shop promises delivery in 30 minutes, you need a way to count how often it keeps that promise. These measurements help count how often a network keeps its promises.

subtitle: Measuring whether network services keep their performance promises.

tldr.problem: Network services are expected to meet performance guarantees (like latency or loss limits), but providers need a standard way to measure and prove compliance with these Service Level Objectives (SLOs).
tldr.mechanism: Precision Availability Metrics (PAMs) divide time into intervals and classify each as meeting the SLO (violation-free), slightly degraded (violated), or severely degraded. This yields metrics like violation ratios and mean time between failures that can be monitored in real time.
tldr.outcome: Providers and customers can now assess SLO compliance automatically, which helps optimize service delivery, detect problems early, and fairly account for the quality delivered.

today: RFC 9544 is an Informational RFC and defines metrics that can be used by service providers and customers to measure SLO compliance. It has not been updated or obsoleted and provides the foundation for monitoring network service quality.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network services such as VPN connections, cloud services, or network slice services offer performance guarantees to their customers. A Service Level Objective (SLO) defines what performance the service should deliver, like "maximum packet delay of 50 milliseconds" or "less than 0.1% packet loss". Service providers and customers need a standard way to measure whether the service is actually meeting these guarantees.

The RFC defines Precision Availability Metrics (PAMs), a set of metrics designed to assess how well a service complies with its SLOs. Unlike raw measurements of latency or loss, PAMs focus on answering the question: Is this service delivering the promised performance right now? They can be used for real-time monitoring, billing, and troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: A promise like "your internet will be fast" needs a way to measure if it's being kept. PAMs are the ruler you use to measure that, checking every second or millisecond to see if the network is keeping its promise.

sections.title: Time Intervals and Violation Categories
sections.content:
PAMs divide time into small intervals (for example, one second each, though any granularity can be chosen). Each interval is classified into one of three categories:

Violation-Free Interval (VFI): all performance parameters are at or better than their defined thresholds (the service is meeting its SLOs). Violated Interval (VI): at least one parameter has degraded below its optimal threshold (the service is not meeting its SLOs). Severely Violated Interval (SVI): at least one parameter has degraded below a critical threshold (the service is in serious trouble).

By counting how many intervals fall into each category, basic metrics are obtained: VI count, SVI count, and VFI count. This simple classification is the foundation for all PAM calculations.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine watching your internet every second: is it good (meeting promises), bad (promises broken), or very bad (almost completely broken)? PAMs count each second as one of those three types.

sections.title: Core Metrics: Ratios and Packet Counts
sections.content:
From the interval categories, two key historical metrics are derived. Violated Interval Ratio (VIR) is the fraction of all intervals that were either VI or SVI—a measure of how often the service failed to meet its SLOs over a measurement period. Severely Violated Interval Ratio (SVIR) is the fraction that were SVI, highlighting the most serious violations.

In addition to counting intervals, the RFC introduces packet counting metrics: Violated Packets Count (VPC) and Severely Violated Packets Count (SVPC). These distinguish between a few packets arriving late and many packets arriving late, which helps assess both instantaneous problems and widespread capacity issues.
sections.plainLanguage: VIR answers "what percentage of time was the service broken?" Packet counts answer "how many messages were affected?" Together they show whether problems were brief spikes or deep, widespread issues.

sections.title: Real-Time Monitoring Metrics
sections.content:
PAMs also include metrics modeled after Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF), which are useful for real-time monitoring. These include time since the last violated interval, the mean time between violated intervals, and the mean number of packets between violated intervals. Analogous metrics exist for severely violated intervals.

These derived metrics help operators see at a glance how stable a service is. A service that has not had a violation in the last hour is reassuring, whereas one that fails every minute is a red flag, regardless of how long the measurement period has been.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time metrics answer "how long has it been since something went wrong?" or "on average, how long do things stay good?". They help network operators spot trouble early.

sections.title: Service Availability States and Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC suggests that PAMs could support a state machine with two states: "available" and "unavailable". A service moves to unavailable after a certain number of successive interval violations (the unavailability threshold) and returns to available after a certain number of violation-free intervals (the availability threshold). The specific thresholds are configured by the service provider.

This configuration approach allows each service to define what "available" means in its context. A video streaming service might tolerate more loss than a trading system, and the thresholds can reflect that difference.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a broken traffic light: you need a few seconds of red light before you say it's broken (unavailability threshold), and you need a few minutes of working correctly before you trust it again (availability threshold).

sections.title: Status and Future Work
sections.content: RFC 9544 is Informational and does not define new protocol messages or modify Internet standards. Rather, it proposes metrics that can be collected and exported by existing mechanisms like IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) or by YANG data models. The RFC notes that additional work is needed: YANG models for configuration, IPFIX information elements for export, and support for statistical SLOs that allow a percentage of packets to exceed thresholds.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is like a blueprint for how to measure; other RFCs and tools will build on it to actually collect and send those measurements.
